A Filtering Antenna With Improved Frequency Selectivity and Wideband
Harmonic Suppression
Chunxu Mao , Yuekun Sun , and Jian Feng Li

path and cross-coupling path will lead to the cancellation of the
power, resulting in radiation nulls at speciﬁc frequencies [21], [22],

Abstract— In this communication, a compact ﬁltering antenna with

high frequency selectivity and intensive harmonic suppression over a
wide frequency range (3 f0) is proposed. The antenna mainly consists
of a planar inverted-F structure (PIFS), a square patch, two parasitic
half-wavelength strips, and a layer of metasurface under the patch. The
PIFS, parasitic strips, and patch are cross-coupled and tuned at their
fundamental mode to produce the third-order ﬁltering response with
enhanced bandwidth and sharp roll-off at band-edges. To suppress the
higher order harmonics, a split ring resonator (SRR) is ﬁrst inset into
the PIFS to reject the main input power. Then, a layer of metasurface is
introduced under the patch to further absorb extra power. As a result, the
radiation efﬁciency at the second-order harmonic can be reduced from
40% to 4%. The principles of the proposed antenna are investigated
in detail. The ﬁltering antenna is prototyped and veriﬁed, exhibiting a
passband from 2.5 to 3.0 GHz and a gain suppression of 24 dB from
3.1 to 6.0 GHz and 18 dB from 6.0 to 9.0 GHz.
Another important issue to be concerned with the ﬁltering

antenna is the harmonic radiation, which can lead to potential
cross-band interference between different wireless applications since
the microwave frequency spectrum is already crowded. A straight-
forward way of suppressing the harmonic radiation is to cascade a
bandpass of low-pass ﬁlter at the feed of the antenna [26], [27], [28].
However, this will lead to additional insertion loss and reduce the sys-
tem’s efﬁciency. By detuning the resonances of high-order modes of
different parts of the antenna, the harmonics in the high-band can be
signiﬁcantly suppressed without affecting the in-band radiation [29],
[30]. Besides, by loading parasitic structures [31], [32] or using a
hybrid feeding network [33], improved out-of-band rejection can be
achieved. In [34], a hybrid approach of combining multiple slots
loading and bandpass ﬁlter is studied, and multiple radiation nulls are
intentionally generated in the speciﬁc bands, leading to a wideband
harmonic suppression of over four times of center frequency (4 f0).
However, most of these works have a limited frequency range of
suppression, or the suppression is not intense enough. In addition,
most of the works only show the broadside realized gain, which is
not sufﬁcient when evaluating the harmonic suppression performance,
as interferences may come from different directions.
Index Terms— Antenna, ﬁltering antenna, frequency selectivity, har-
monic suppression, meta-surface.
I. INTRODUCTION
Filtering antennas can simultaneously function as antennas and

ﬁlters, leading to a signiﬁcant reduction of complexity and cost of
RF frontends and improvement of overall frequency responses, and
hence, have been a popular research topic in the last decades [1].
Various of antennas with integrated ﬁltering performance are pro-
posed, such as wideband ﬁltering antennas [2], [3], dual-band ﬁltering
antennas [4], [5], dual-polarization ﬁltering antennas [6], [7], [8],
circular-polarized ﬁltering antennas [9], [10], and millimeter-wave
ﬁltering antennas [11], [12], [13]. Besides, the ﬁltering antennas with
low-proﬁle [14], [15], [16] and duplexing/multiplexing functions [17],
[18] are investigated. To replace traditional scenarios of cascaded
ﬁlter and antenna in the RF frontend system, the ﬁltering antennas
with high frequency selectivity and harmonic suppression are highly
desired.
In this communication, an innovative ﬁltering antenna features of

high frequency selectivity and wideband harmonic suppression is
proposed. By symmetrically placing two resonant structures beside
the driven planar inverted-F structure (PIFS), an additional in-band
resonant mode and a radiation null can be generated simultaneously,
leading to an improved bandwidth and frequency selectivity at the
band-edge. The method of controlling radiation null is analyzed in
detail. Furthermore, an effective approach to suppressing harmonic
radiation is studied step-by-step. First, a split ring resonator (SRR) is
inset into the feed PIFS to introduce impedance mismatch in the band
of harmonic, resulting in most of the input power reﬂected back at the
port. Then, a metasurface is loaded below the patch radiator, sharing
the same layer with the PIFS, and the harmonic radiation can be
further reduced to around 4% without affecting the in-band radiation
efﬁciency. It should be noticed that the parameters of peak realized
gain and radiation efﬁciency are used in the analysis in this communi-
cation to provide a fair way to evaluate the ﬁltering performance. The
proposed ﬁltering antenna is prototyped and veriﬁed experimentally,
showing an improved frequency selectivity and harmonic suppression.
The frequency selectivity represents the ability of suppressing the

interference from adjacent bands, which can usually be achieved by
integrating ﬁlters at the feeds of antennas or introducing radiation
nulls at the band-edges. In [19] and [20], bandpass ﬁlters are
integrated with antennas, and good frequency selectivity can be
achieved by the resonators. However, these added resonators will
lead to extra insertion loss. Another popular method of improving the
frequency selectivity is to conﬁgure the cross-coupling path between

III. WIDEBAND HARMONIC SUPPRESSION
For a ﬁltering antenna, another important issue to be concerned

with is the cross-band interference due to the radiation of the higher
order modes, especially for the second-order harmonics, which are
not far away from the predominant mode and usually very strong.
In this section, different methods, including an embedded SRR and
metasurface layer, are combined to suppress the harmonic radiation
over a wide frequency range.
A. Embedded SRR
To suppress the radiation of the second-order harmonic, a SRR

is embedded into the PIFS, as shown in Fig. 7(a). The resonant
frequency of the SRR is tuned to the second-order harmonic of the
proposed ﬁltering antenna, at around 5.6 GHz. Fig. 8 compares the
simulated current distribution at 5.6 GHz between the Type-C and
Type-D antennas. As observed from Fig. 8(a), when the PIFS and
the parasitic strip resonators are working at the second-order mode,
intensive power can be coupled from PIFS to the strip resonators.
When the SRR is embedded into the PIFS, which is resonant at
around 5.6 GHz, an intensive current is distributed around the SRR.
Hence, the power coupled to the two parasitic strip resonators can be
signiﬁcantly reduced. Since the majority power is reﬂected back on
the PIFS, the second-order harmonic can be efﬁciently suppressed.
Fig. 9 compares the simulated peak realized gain and radiation

efﬁciency among the reference antennas Type-C, Type-D, Type-E,
and the proposed antenna. It is noted that the peak realized gain
instead of the realized gain in the broadside direction is adopted
to measure the harmonic suppression performance as the cross-band
interference may originally come from any direction, but not only
from the broadside direction. As observed from Fig. 9(a), the peak
realized gain of the second-order harmonic is reduced from 6 dBi to
below 0 dBi from the Type-C antenna to the Type-D antenna, and
the radiation efﬁciency is reduced from 40% to 14%.
B. Metasurface for Harmonic Suppression
Although most of the input power of the second-order harmonic is

reﬂected back at the PIFS, there are still some power couples from
the PIFS to the patch and radiate out. To further suppress unwanted
radiation, a new method of loading a layer of metasurface below the
radiator is proposed, as shown in Fig. 7(b). The metasurface is placed
on the upper layer of the bottom substrate without introducing addi-
tional substrate/layer. The conﬁguration of the unit cell is presented
in Fig. 10(a), which is simply a patch shorted to the ground plane
through a pin. The opened sides of the patch are equivalent to a
capacitor, whereas the shorted pin can be molded as an inductor; the
lossy substrate is represented by a resistor. Thus, the unit cell can
be viewed as a series resonant circuit, and the resonant frequency
can be controlled by tuning the gap between the unit cells. When it
resonates, an intensive E-ﬁeld distribution will be generated, leading
to the loss of power. As a result, the power in the designed frequency
can be suppressed [35].
A periodic boundary is used to investigate the resonance of the unit

cell, as shown in Fig. 10(b). As observed, the resonance is moved to
the lower band when L4 is increased. The resonance here indicates
that a small part of the incident wave is absorbed and lost in the unit
cell when it resonates, but it is insufﬁcient to deal with high-power
cases when it works alone, as the Type-E curve shown in Fig. 9.
However, this additional structure can be used to further suppress the
radiation in the given frequency range. As depicted in Fig. 9, the peak
realized gain at the second-order harmonic can be reduced by 14 dB
when rejection bands of the SRR and the metasurface are aligned with
each other. Analyzing the radiation efﬁciency in Fig. 9(b), the power

radiated out is further suppressed to below 4% when the metasurface
is applied, demonstrating that a good harmonic suppression can be
achieved.
For better presenting the harmonic suppression performance, the

simulated E-ﬁeld distributions of the antenna are displayed and com-
pared in Fig. 11. As shown in Fig. 11(a), although a major power of
the second-order harmonic has been reﬂected back at the input, there
are still some power coupled to the radiating patch, which is working
at its high-order mode. When the metasurface is placed below the
radiating patch, the power that is coupled to the radiating patch is
much weaker than that the one without a metasurface, as shown in
Fig. 11(b). Having another check of the E-ﬁeld distribution on the
upper layer of the bottom substrate, an intensive E-ﬁeld is distributed
along the gaps between the unit cell without producing an effective
radiation, which veriﬁes our supposition. Therefore, by combining
the embedded SRR in the PIFS and loading a layer of metasurface,
the radiation of the harmonics can be signiﬁcantly suppressed.

The proposed ﬁltering antenna was fabricated, and the upper layers

of the bottom and top substrates of the prototype are respectively
shown in Fig. 12. As shown in Fig. 12(a), from inner to outer,
they are PIFS with embedded SRR, two parasitic strip resonators,
and a layer of metasurface surrounding. The copper areas of the
two layers are similar, and thus, a compact size can be maintained.
Fig. 13(a) presents the measured and simulated S-parameters from

realized gains and the radiation efﬁciency of the proposed ﬁltering
antenna. Similarly, a good consistence can be observed between the

V. CONCLUSION
In this communication, a compact ﬁltering antenna with improved

frequency selectivity and wideband harmonic suppression has been
proposed for wireless applications. By conﬁguring a cross-coupling,
a radiation null can be realized at the band-edge for enhancing the
frequency selectivity. To suppress the radiation from harmonics over
a wide frequency range, a slit ring resonator is ﬁrst embedded into the
feed source. Then, a metasurface is employed to further reduce the
harmonic radiation for the ﬁrst time. The principles of generating
and controlling the radiation null, as well as the procedure of
suppressing harmonics, have been explained in detail. Compared with
other reported works, the proposed ﬁltering antenna has shown an
improved frequency selectivity and wideband harmonic suppression
performance. The techniques developed in this work can be widely
used in other types of antennas.

suppressing harmonics, have been explained in detail. Compared with
other reported works, the proposed ﬁltering antenna has shown an
improved frequency selectivity and wideband harmonic suppression
performance. The techniques developed in this work can be widely
used in other types of antennas.

sections.heading: I. INTRODUCTION
sections.content:
Filtering antennas can simultaneously function as antennas and

ﬁlters, leading to a signiﬁcant reduction of complexity and cost of
RF frontends and improvement of overall frequency responses, and
hence, have been a popular research topic in the last decades [1].
Various of antennas with integrated ﬁltering performance are pro-
posed, such as wideband ﬁltering antennas [2], [3], dual-band ﬁltering
antennas [4], [5], dual-polarization ﬁltering antennas [6], [7], [8],
circular-polarized ﬁltering antennas [9], [10], and millimeter-wave
ﬁltering antennas [11], [12], [13]. Besides, the ﬁltering antennas with
low-proﬁle [14], [15], [16] and duplexing/multiplexing functions [17],
[18] are investigated. To replace traditional scenarios of cascaded
ﬁlter and antenna in the RF frontend system, the ﬁltering antennas
with high frequency selectivity and harmonic suppression are highly
desired.

The frequency selectivity represents the ability of suppressing the

interference from adjacent bands, which can usually be achieved by
integrating ﬁlters at the feeds of antennas or introducing radiation
nulls at the band-edges. In [19] and [20], bandpass ﬁlters are
integrated with antennas, and good frequency selectivity can be
achieved by the resonators. However, these added resonators will
lead to extra insertion loss. Another popular method of improving the
frequency selectivity is to conﬁgure the cross-coupling path between

the feed and radiator; the out-of-phase between the main coupling
path and cross-coupling path will lead to the cancellation of the
power, resulting in radiation nulls at speciﬁc frequencies [21], [22],
[23]. By adjusting the coupling intensity, the radiation nulls can be
easily controlled. In addition, single or multiple radiation nulls can
be generated by slitting slots in the radiating element [24] or using
a reverse feeding method [25].

Another important issue to be concerned with the ﬁltering

antenna is the harmonic radiation, which can lead to potential
cross-band interference between different wireless applications since
the microwave frequency spectrum is already crowded. A straight-
forward way of suppressing the harmonic radiation is to cascade a
bandpass of low-pass ﬁlter at the feed of the antenna [26], [27], [28].
However, this will lead to additional insertion loss and reduce the sys-
tem’s efﬁciency. By detuning the resonances of high-order modes of
different parts of the antenna, the harmonics in the high-band can be
signiﬁcantly suppressed without affecting the in-band radiation [29],
[30]. Besides, by loading parasitic structures [31], [32] or using a
hybrid feeding network [33], improved out-of-band rejection can be
achieved. In [34], a hybrid approach of combining multiple slots
loading and bandpass ﬁlter is studied, and multiple radiation nulls are
intentionally generated in the speciﬁc bands, leading to a wideband
harmonic suppression of over four times of center frequency (4 f0).
However, most of these works have a limited frequency range of
suppression, or the suppression is not intense enough. In addition,
most of the works only show the broadside realized gain, which is
not sufﬁcient when evaluating the harmonic suppression performance,
as interferences may come from different directions.

In this communication, an innovative ﬁltering antenna features of

high frequency selectivity and wideband harmonic suppression is
proposed. By symmetrically placing two resonant structures beside
the driven planar inverted-F structure (PIFS), an additional in-band
resonant mode and a radiation null can be generated simultaneously,
leading to an improved bandwidth and frequency selectivity at the
band-edge. The method of controlling radiation null is analyzed in
detail. Furthermore, an effective approach to suppressing harmonic
radiation is studied step-by-step. First, a split ring resonator (SRR) is
inset into the feed PIFS to introduce impedance mismatch in the band
of harmonic, resulting in most of the input power reﬂected back at the
port. Then, a metasurface is loaded below the patch radiator, sharing
the same layer with the PIFS, and the harmonic radiation can be
further reduced to around 4% without affecting the in-band radiation
efﬁciency. It should be noticed that the parameters of peak realized
gain and radiation efﬁciency are used in the analysis in this communi-
cation to provide a fair way to evaluate the ﬁltering performance. The
proposed ﬁltering antenna is prototyped and veriﬁed experimentally,
showing an improved frequency selectivity and harmonic suppression.

ﬁltering response. Section III discusses the methods of realizing the

sections.heading: B. Design Procedures
sections.content:
To better illustrate the design procedure of the ﬁltering antenna,

three referenced antennas and their corresponding topologies, denoted
as Type-A, B, and C, are presented in Fig. 2. The antenna design
is originally from a traditional proximate-fed patch antenna (Type-
A), as shown in Fig. 2(a). Here, the patch antenna is equivalent
to a resonator, R1, and the radiation in free space is viewed as a
load. Since only the dominant mode is concerned and excited, the
Type-A reference antenna has shown only one resonant frequency
at around 2.6 GHz, leading to a limited bandwidth of 100 MHz,
as shown in Fig. 3. When the microstrip feed is replaced by a
PIFS through shorting one end of the microstrip to the ground,
a second-order resonant structure can be achieved, as the topology

presented. The resonances of the patch and the PIFS are tuned to
similar frequency, resulting in a second-order frequency response with
improved bandwidth of 300 MHz. By further loading two parasitic
strip resonators (denoted as R3 and R3′) around the PIFS, as depicted
in Fig. 2(c), one more resonant frequency can be realized, rendering
a third-order frequency response with an improved bandwidth of
over 500 MHz. In addition, the parasitic strips can conﬁgure a
cross-coupling path with a 180◦phase behind the main coupling
path. When the power from the two coupling paths is comparable
at a given frequency, the power will be canceled out, leading to a
radiation null. As shown in Fig. 3, the radiation null is generated at
3.1 GHz, resulting in a sharp roll-off from the bandpass to band-stop
at the higher band-edge. An approximate calculation shows that the
roll-off is over 218 dB/GHz, which is comparable to a ﬁlter.

sections.heading: III. WIDEBAND HARMONIC SUPPRESSION
sections.content:
For a ﬁltering antenna, another important issue to be concerned

with is the cross-band interference due to the radiation of the higher
order modes, especially for the second-order harmonics, which are
not far away from the predominant mode and usually very strong.
In this section, different methods, including an embedded SRR and
metasurface layer, are combined to suppress the harmonic radiation
over a wide frequency range.

For better presenting the harmonic suppression performance, the

simulated E-ﬁeld distributions of the antenna are displayed and com-
pared in Fig. 11. As shown in Fig. 11(a), although a major power of
the second-order harmonic has been reﬂected back at the input, there
are still some power coupled to the radiating patch, which is working
at its high-order mode. When the metasurface is placed below the
radiating patch, the power that is coupled to the radiating patch is
much weaker than that the one without a metasurface, as shown in
Fig. 11(b). Having another check of the E-ﬁeld distribution on the
upper layer of the bottom substrate, an intensive E-ﬁeld is distributed
along the gaps between the unit cell without producing an effective
radiation, which veriﬁes our supposition. Therefore, by combining
the embedded SRR in the PIFS and loading a layer of metasurface,
the radiation of the harmonics can be signiﬁcantly suppressed.

sections.heading: A. Embedded SRR
sections.content:
To suppress the radiation of the second-order harmonic, a SRR

is embedded into the PIFS, as shown in Fig. 7(a). The resonant
frequency of the SRR is tuned to the second-order harmonic of the
proposed ﬁltering antenna, at around 5.6 GHz. Fig. 8 compares the
simulated current distribution at 5.6 GHz between the Type-C and
Type-D antennas. As observed from Fig. 8(a), when the PIFS and
the parasitic strip resonators are working at the second-order mode,
intensive power can be coupled from PIFS to the strip resonators.
When the SRR is embedded into the PIFS, which is resonant at
around 5.6 GHz, an intensive current is distributed around the SRR.
Hence, the power coupled to the two parasitic strip resonators can be
signiﬁcantly reduced. Since the majority power is reﬂected back on
the PIFS, the second-order harmonic can be efﬁciently suppressed.

and the proposed antenna. It is noted that the peak realized gain
instead of the realized gain in the broadside direction is adopted
to measure the harmonic suppression performance as the cross-band
interference may originally come from any direction, but not only
from the broadside direction. As observed from Fig. 9(a), the peak

sections.heading: B. Metasurface for Harmonic Suppression
sections.content:
Although most of the input power of the second-order harmonic is

reﬂected back at the PIFS, there are still some power couples from
the PIFS to the patch and radiate out. To further suppress unwanted
radiation, a new method of loading a layer of metasurface below the
radiator is proposed, as shown in Fig. 7(b). The metasurface is placed
on the upper layer of the bottom substrate without introducing addi-
tional substrate/layer. The conﬁguration of the unit cell is presented
in Fig. 10(a), which is simply a patch shorted to the ground plane
through a pin. The opened sides of the patch are equivalent to a
capacitor, whereas the shorted pin can be molded as an inductor; the
lossy substrate is represented by a resistor. Thus, the unit cell can
be viewed as a series resonant circuit, and the resonant frequency
can be controlled by tuning the gap between the unit cells. When it
resonates, an intensive E-ﬁeld distribution will be generated, leading
to the loss of power. As a result, the power in the designed frequency
can be suppressed [35].

A periodic boundary is used to investigate the resonance of the unit

cell, as shown in Fig. 10(b). As observed, the resonance is moved to
the lower band when L4 is increased. The resonance here indicates
that a small part of the incident wave is absorbed and lost in the unit
cell when it resonates, but it is insufﬁcient to deal with high-power
cases when it works alone, as the Type-E curve shown in Fig. 9.
However, this additional structure can be used to further suppress the
radiation in the given frequency range. As depicted in Fig. 9, the peak
realized gain at the second-order harmonic can be reduced by 14 dB
when rejection bands of the SRR and the metasurface are aligned with
each other. Analyzing the radiation efﬁciency in Fig. 9(b), the power

radiated out is further suppressed to below 4% when the metasurface
is applied, demonstrating that a good harmonic suppression can be
achieved.

sections.heading: IV. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
sections.content:
The proposed ﬁltering antenna was fabricated, and the upper layers

of the bottom and top substrates of the prototype are respectively
shown in Fig. 12. As shown in Fig. 12(a), from inner to outer,
they are PIFS with embedded SRR, two parasitic strip resonators,
and a layer of metasurface surrounding. The copper areas of the
two layers are similar, and thus, a compact size can be maintained.
Fig. 13(a) presents the measured and simulated S-parameters from
1.5 to 9 GHz. As observed, the measured results agree well with
the simulations in terms of impedance match and gain response.
The measured impedance −10 dB bandwidth of the antenna is from
2.4 to 2.9 GHz. Outside of the band, the reﬂection coefﬁcients are
close to 0 dB. Fig. 13(b) displays the simulated and measured peak
realized gains and the radiation efﬁciency of the proposed ﬁltering
antenna. Similarly, a good consistence can be observed between the
simulated and measured results. As can be seen, the measured peak
realized gains are about 8 dBi in the band, which is quickly reduced
to below −15 dBi from 3 to 5.8 GHz, giving a harmonic suppression
of over 23 dB. The realized gain is somehow increased in the band of
6.0–9.0 GHz, but still remains over 18 dB gain suppression. This is
mainly due to the mismatch between the higher order resonance of the
patch and the PIFS. The minor discrepancy between the simulated
and measured results at around 6 GHz is mainly attributed to the
fabrication tolerances. Besides, the antenna has a high efﬁciency of
around 90% in the band, but it is basically remained below 8% out
of the band from 3.0 to 9.0 GHz, showing an excellent harmonic
suppression performance.

tion patterns of the proposed antenna at 2.6 GHz. The antenna
exhibits uni-directional radiation pattern in the broadside direction.
The cross-polarization level is more than 30 dB lower than in the
co-polarization. In addition, the front-to-back ratio is over 20 dB,
showing the proposed antenna has a good radiation performance.
The small discrepancy between the simulated and measured radiation
patterns is mainly due to the tolerances during the measurement.

The proposed antenna is compared with other ﬁltering antennas

with harmonic suppression performance reported in [26], [27], [28],
[29], [30], [31], [32], [33], and [34] in terms of antenna proﬁle,
method of suppression, gain in-band, frequency selectivity, and gain
suppression. The antennas in [32] and [33] have a limited bandwidth
of suppression of less than 2 f0, without tackling the second-order
harmonics. The works in [26] and [27] have a wideband harmonic
suppression, but a low in-band gain of less than 3 dBi can be
achieved. The works in [28], [31], and [33] have a limited frequency
selectivity with the roll-off ratio less than 60 dB/GHz. The work

6
IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON ANTENNAS AND PROPAGATION

in [34] has a high gain in-band, good frequency selectivity, and
wideband gain suppression, but the antenna has a high proﬁle.
Compared with these works, the proposed ﬁltering antenna has
a low proﬁle, an improved frequency selectivity, and out-of-band
rejection, and this is the ﬁrst time that resonator and metasurface
are combined together to realize wideband harmonic suppression.
Moreover, different from other works, the peak realized gain instead
of realized in the broadside direction is used to evaluate the harmonic
suppression performance.

sections.heading: V. CONCLUSION
sections.content:
In this communication, a compact ﬁltering antenna with improved

frequency selectivity and wideband harmonic suppression has been
proposed for wireless applications. By conﬁguring a cross-coupling,
a radiation null can be realized at the band-edge for enhancing the
frequency selectivity. To suppress the radiation from harmonics over
a wide frequency range, a slit ring resonator is ﬁrst embedded into the
feed source. Then, a metasurface is employed to further reduce the
harmonic radiation for the ﬁrst time. The principles of generating
and controlling the radiation null, as well as the procedure of
suppressing harmonics, have been explained in detail. Compared with
other reported works, the proposed ﬁltering antenna has shown an
improved frequency selectivity and wideband harmonic suppression
performance. The techniques developed in this work can be widely
used in other types of antennas.

Abstract— In this communication, a compact ﬁltering antenna with
high frequency selectivity and intensive harmonic suppression over a
wide frequency range (3 f0) is proposed. The antenna mainly consists
of a planar inverted-F structure (PIFS), a square patch, two parasitic
half-wavelength strips, and a layer of metasurface under the patch. The
PIFS, parasitic strips, and patch are cross-coupled and tuned at their
fundamental mode to produce the third-order ﬁltering response with
enhanced bandwidth and sharp roll-off at band-edges. To suppress the
higher order harmonics, a split ring resonator (SRR) is ﬁrst inset into
the PIFS to reject the main input power. Then, a layer of metasurface is
introduced under the patch to further absorb extra power. As a result, the
radiation efﬁciency at the second-order harmonic can be reduced from
40% to 4%. The principles of the proposed antenna are investigated
in detail. The ﬁltering antenna is prototyped and veriﬁed, exhibiting a
passband from 2.5 to 3.0 GHz and a gain suppression of 24 dB from
3.1 to 6.0 GHz and 18 dB from 6.0 to 9.0 GHz.
Another important issue to be concerned with the ﬁltering
antenna is the harmonic radiation, which can lead to potential
cross-band interference between different wireless applications since
the microwave frequency spectrum is already crowded. A straight-
forward way of suppressing the harmonic radiation is to cascade a
bandpass of low-pass ﬁlter at the feed of the antenna [26], [27], [28].
However, this will lead to additional insertion loss and reduce the sys-
tem’s efﬁciency. By detuning the resonances of high-order modes of
different parts of the antenna, the harmonics in the high-band can be
signiﬁcantly suppressed without affecting the in-band radiation [29],
[30]. Besides, by loading parasitic structures [31], [32] or using a
hybrid feeding network [33], improved out-of-band rejection can be
achieved. In [34], a hybrid approach of combining multiple slots
loading and bandpass ﬁlter is studied, and multiple radiation nulls are
intentionally generated in the speciﬁc bands, leading to a wideband
harmonic suppression of over four times of center frequency (4 f0).
However, most of these works have a limited frequency range of
suppression, or the suppression is not intense enough. In addition,
most of the works only show the broadside realized gain, which is
not sufﬁcient when evaluating the harmonic suppression performance,
as interferences may come from different directions.
Index Terms— Antenna, ﬁltering antenna, frequency selectivity, har-
monic suppression, meta-surface.
I. INTRODUCTION
Filtering antennas can simultaneously function as antennas and
ﬁlters, leading to a signiﬁcant reduction of complexity and cost of
RF frontends and improvement of overall frequency responses, and
hence, have been a popular research topic in the last decades [1].
Various of antennas with integrated ﬁltering performance are pro-
posed, such as wideband ﬁltering antennas [2], [3], dual-band ﬁltering
antennas [4], [5], dual-polarization ﬁltering antennas [6], [7], [8],
circular-polarized ﬁltering antennas [9], [10], and millimeter-wave
ﬁltering antennas [11], [12], [13]. Besides, the ﬁltering antennas with
low-proﬁle [14], [15], [16] and duplexing/multiplexing functions [17],
[18] are investigated. To replace traditional scenarios of cascaded
ﬁlter and antenna in the RF frontend system, the ﬁltering antennas
with high frequency selectivity and harmonic suppression are highly
desired.
In this communication, an innovative ﬁltering antenna features of
high frequency selectivity and wideband harmonic suppression is
proposed. By symmetrically placing two resonant structures beside
the driven planar inverted-F structure (PIFS), an additional in-band
resonant mode and a radiation null can be generated simultaneously,
leading to an improved bandwidth and frequency selectivity at the
band-edge. The method of controlling radiation null is analyzed in
detail. Furthermore, an effective approach to suppressing harmonic
radiation is studied step-by-step. First, a split ring resonator (SRR) is
inset into the feed PIFS to introduce impedance mismatch in the band
of harmonic, resulting in most of the input power reﬂected back at the
port. Then, a metasurface is loaded below the patch radiator, sharing
the same layer with the PIFS, and the harmonic radiation can be
further reduced to around 4% without affecting the in-band radiation
efﬁciency. It should be noticed that the parameters of peak realized
gain and radiation efﬁciency are used in the analysis in this communi-
cation to provide a fair way to evaluate the ﬁltering performance. The
proposed ﬁltering antenna is prototyped and veriﬁed experimentally,
showing an improved frequency selectivity and harmonic suppression.
The frequency selectivity represents the ability of suppressing the
interference from adjacent bands, which can usually be achieved by
integrating ﬁlters at the feeds of antennas or introducing radiation
nulls at the band-edges. In [19] and [20], bandpass ﬁlters are
integrated with antennas, and good frequency selectivity can be
achieved by the resonators. However, these added resonators will
lead to extra insertion loss. Another popular method of improving the
frequency selectivity is to conﬁgure the cross-coupling path between

III. WIDEBAND HARMONIC SUPPRESSION
For a ﬁltering antenna, another important issue to be concerned
with is the cross-band interference due to the radiation of the higher
order modes, especially for the second-order harmonics, which are
not far away from the predominant mode and usually very strong.
In this section, different methods, including an embedded SRR and
metasurface layer, are combined to suppress the harmonic radiation
over a wide frequency range.
A. Embedded SRR
To suppress the radiation of the second-order harmonic, a SRR
is embedded into the PIFS, as shown in Fig. 7(a). The resonant
frequency of the SRR is tuned to the second-order harmonic of the
proposed ﬁltering antenna, at around 5.6 GHz. Fig. 8 compares the
simulated current distribution at 5.6 GHz between the Type-C and
Type-D antennas. As observed from Fig. 8(a), when the PIFS and
the parasitic strip resonators are working at the second-order mode,
intensive power can be coupled from PIFS to the strip resonators.
When the SRR is embedded into the PIFS, which is resonant at
around 5.6 GHz, an intensive current is distributed around the SRR.
Hence, the power coupled to the two parasitic strip resonators can be
signiﬁcantly reduced. Since the majority power is reﬂected back on
the PIFS, the second-order harmonic can be efﬁciently suppressed.
Fig. 9 compares the simulated peak realized gain and radiation
efﬁciency among the reference antennas Type-C, Type-D, Type-E,
and the proposed antenna. It is noted that the peak realized gain
instead of the realized gain in the broadside direction is adopted
to measure the harmonic suppression performance as the cross-band
interference may originally come from any direction, but not only
from the broadside direction. As observed from Fig. 9(a), the peak
realized gain of the second-order harmonic is reduced from 6 dBi to
below 0 dBi from the Type-C antenna to the Type-D antenna, and
the radiation efﬁciency is reduced from 40% to 14%.
B. Metasurface for Harmonic Suppression
Although most of the input power of the second-order harmonic is
reﬂected back at the PIFS, there are still some power couples from
the PIFS to the patch and radiate out. To further suppress unwanted
radiation, a new method of loading a layer of metasurface below the
radiator is proposed, as shown in Fig. 7(b). The metasurface is placed
on the upper layer of the bottom substrate without introducing addi-
tional substrate/layer. The conﬁguration of the unit cell is presented
in Fig. 10(a), which is simply a patch shorted to the ground plane
through a pin. The opened sides of the patch are equivalent to a
capacitor, whereas the shorted pin can be molded as an inductor; the
lossy substrate is represented by a resistor. Thus, the unit cell can
be viewed as a series resonant circuit, and the resonant frequency
can be controlled by tuning the gap between the unit cells. When it
resonates, an intensive E-ﬁeld distribution will be generated, leading
to the loss of power. As a result, the power in the designed frequency
can be suppressed [35].
A periodic boundary is used to investigate the resonance of the unit
cell, as shown in Fig. 10(b). As observed, the resonance is moved to
the lower band when L4 is increased. The resonance here indicates
that a small part of the incident wave is absorbed and lost in the unit
cell when it resonates, but it is insufﬁcient to deal with high-power
cases when it works alone, as the Type-E curve shown in Fig. 9.
However, this additional structure can be used to further suppress the
radiation in the given frequency range. As depicted in Fig. 9, the peak
realized gain at the second-order harmonic can be reduced by 14 dB
when rejection bands of the SRR and the metasurface are aligned with
each other. Analyzing the radiation efﬁciency in Fig. 9(b), the power
radiated out is further suppressed to below 4% when the metasurface
is applied, demonstrating that a good harmonic suppression can be
achieved.
For better presenting the harmonic suppression performance, the
simulated E-ﬁeld distributions of the antenna are displayed and com-
pared in Fig. 11. As shown in Fig. 11(a), although a major power of
the second-order harmonic has been reﬂected back at the input, there
are still some power coupled to the radiating patch, which is working
at its high-order mode. When the metasurface is placed below the
radiating patch, the power that is coupled to the radiating patch is
much weaker than that the one without a metasurface, as shown in
Fig. 11(b). Having another check of the E-ﬁeld distribution on the
upper layer of the bottom substrate, an intensive E-ﬁeld is distributed
along the gaps between the unit cell without producing an effective
radiation, which veriﬁes our supposition. Therefore, by combining
the embedded SRR in the PIFS and loading a layer of metasurface,
the radiation of the harmonics can be signiﬁcantly suppressed.
IV. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
The proposed ﬁltering antenna was fabricated, and the upper layers
of the bottom and top substrates of the prototype are respectively
shown in Fig. 12. As shown in Fig. 12(a), from inner to outer,
they are PIFS with embedded SRR, two parasitic strip resonators,
and a layer of metasurface surrounding. The copper areas of the
two layers are similar, and thus, a compact size can be maintained.
Fig. 13(a) presents the measured and simulated S-parameters from
1.5 to 9 GHz. As observed, the measured results agree well with
the simulations in terms of impedance match and gain response.
The measured impedance −10 dB bandwidth of the antenna is from
2.4 to 2.9 GHz. Outside of the band, the reﬂection coefﬁcients are
close to 0 dB. Fig. 13(b) displays the simulated and measured peak
realized gains and the radiation efﬁciency of the proposed ﬁltering
antenna. Similarly, a good consistence can be observed between the
simulated and measured results. As can be seen, the measured peak
realized gains are about 8 dBi in the band, which is quickly reduced
to below −15 dBi from 3 to 5.8 GHz, giving a harmonic suppression
of over 23 dB. The realized gain is somehow increased in the band of
6.0–9.0 GHz, but still remains over 18 dB gain suppression. This is
mainly due to the mismatch between the higher order resonance of the
patch and the PIFS. The minor discrepancy between the simulated
and measured results at around 6 GHz is mainly attributed to the
fabrication tolerances. Besides, the antenna has a high efﬁciency of
around 90% in the band, but it is basically remained below 8% out
of the band from 3.0 to 9.0 GHz, showing an excellent harmonic
suppression performance.
Fig. 14 shows the simulated and measured normalized radia-
tion patterns of the proposed antenna at 2.6 GHz. The antenna
exhibits uni-directional radiation pattern in the broadside direction.
The cross-polarization level is more than 30 dB lower than in the
co-polarization. In addition, the front-to-back ratio is over 20 dB,
showing the proposed antenna has a good radiation performance.
The small discrepancy between the simulated and measured radiation
patterns is mainly due to the tolerances during the measurement.
The proposed antenna is compared with other ﬁltering antennas
with harmonic suppression performance reported in [26], [27], [28],
[29], [30], [31], [32], [33], and [34] in terms of antenna proﬁle,
method of suppression, gain in-band, frequency selectivity, and gain
suppression. The antennas in [32] and [33] have a limited bandwidth
of suppression of less than 2 f0, without tackling the second-order
harmonics. The works in [26] and [27] have a wideband harmonic
suppression, but a low in-band gain of less than 3 dBi can be
achieved. The works in [28], [31], and [33] have a limited frequency
selectivity with the roll-off ratio less than 60 dB/GHz. The work

in [34] has a high gain in-band, good frequency selectivity, and
wideband gain suppression, but the antenna has a high proﬁle.
Compared with these works, the proposed ﬁltering antenna has
a low proﬁle, an improved frequency selectivity, and out-of-band
rejection, and this is the ﬁrst time that resonator and metasurface
are combined together to realize wideband harmonic suppression.
Moreover, different from other works, the peak realized gain instead
of realized in the broadside direction is used to evaluate the harmonic
suppression performance.
V. CONCLUSION
In this communication, a compact ﬁltering antenna with improved
frequency selectivity and wideband harmonic suppression has been
proposed for wireless applications. By conﬁguring a cross-coupling,
a radiation null can be realized at the band-edge for enhancing the
frequency selectivity. To suppress the radiation from harmonics over
a wide frequency range, a slit ring resonator is ﬁrst embedded into the
feed source. Then, a metasurface is employed to further reduce the
harmonic radiation for the ﬁrst time. The principles of generating
and controlling the radiation null, as well as the procedure of
suppressing harmonics, have been explained in detail. Compared with
other reported works, the proposed ﬁltering antenna has shown an
improved frequency selectivity and wideband harmonic suppression
performance. The techniques developed in this work can be widely
used in other types of antennas.

Abstract— In this communication, a compact ﬁltering antenna with
high frequency selectivity and intensive harmonic suppression over a
wide frequency range (3 f0) is proposed. The antenna mainly consists
of a planar inverted-F structure (PIFS), a square patch, two parasitic
half-wavelength strips, and a layer of metasurface under the patch. The
PIFS, parasitic strips, and patch are cross-coupled and tuned at their
fundamental mode to produce the third-order ﬁltering response with
enhanced bandwidth and sharp roll-off at band-edges. To suppress the
higher order harmonics, a split ring resonator (SRR) is ﬁrst inset into
the PIFS to reject the main input power. Then, a layer of metasurface is
introduced under the patch to further absorb extra power. As a result, the
radiation efﬁciency at the second-order harmonic can be reduced from
40% to 4%. The principles of the proposed antenna are investigated
in detail. The ﬁltering antenna is prototyped and veriﬁed, exhibiting a
passband from 2.5 to 3.0 GHz and a gain suppression of 24 dB from
3.1 to 6.0 GHz and 18 dB from 6.0 to 9.0 GHz.
Another important issue to be concerned with the ﬁltering
antenna is the harmonic radiation, which can lead to potential
cross-band interference between different wireless applications since
the microwave frequency spectrum is already crowded. A straight-
forward way of suppressing the harmonic radiation is to cascade a
bandpass of low-pass ﬁlter at the feed of the antenna [26], [27], [28].
However, this will lead to additional insertion loss and reduce the sys-
tem’s efﬁciency. By detuning the resonances of high-order modes of
different parts of the antenna, the harmonics in the high-band can be
signiﬁcantly suppressed without affecting the in-band radiation [29],
[30]. Besides, by loading parasitic structures [31], [32] or using a
hybrid feeding network [33], improved out-of-band rejection can be
achieved. In [34], a hybrid approach of combining multiple slots
loading and bandpass ﬁlter is studied, and multiple radiation nulls are
intentionally generated in the speciﬁc bands, leading to a wideband
harmonic suppression of over four times of center frequency (4 f0).
However, most of these works have a limited frequency range of
suppression, or the suppression is not intense enough. In addition,
most of the works only show the broadside realized gain, which is
not sufﬁcient when evaluating the harmonic suppression performance,
as interferences may come from different directions.
Index Terms— Antenna, ﬁltering antenna, frequency selectivity, har-
monic suppression, meta-surface.
I. INTRODUCTION
Filtering antennas can simultaneously function as antennas and
ﬁlters, leading to a signiﬁcant reduction of complexity and cost of
RF frontends and improvement of overall frequency responses, and
hence, have been a popular research topic in the last decades [1].
Various of antennas with integrated ﬁltering performance are pro-
posed, such as wideband ﬁltering antennas [2], [3], dual-band ﬁltering
antennas [4], [5], dual-polarization ﬁltering antennas [6], [7], [8],
circular-polarized ﬁltering antennas [9], [10], and millimeter-wave
ﬁltering antennas [11], [12], [13]. Besides, the ﬁltering antennas with
low-proﬁle [14], [15], [16] and duplexing/multiplexing functions [17],
[18] are investigated. To replace traditional scenarios of cascaded
ﬁlter and antenna in the RF frontend system, the ﬁltering antennas
with high frequency selectivity and harmonic suppression are highly
desired.
In this communication, an innovative ﬁltering antenna features of
high frequency selectivity and wideband harmonic suppression is
proposed. By symmetrically placing two resonant structures beside
the driven planar inverted-F structure (PIFS), an additional in-band

efﬁciency. It should be noticed that the parameters of peak realized

proposed ﬁltering antenna is prototyped and veriﬁed experimentally,
showing an improved frequency selectivity and harmonic suppression.

III. WIDEBAND HARMONIC SUPPRESSION
For a ﬁltering antenna, another important issue to be concerned
with is the cross-band interference due to the radiation of the higher
order modes, especially for the second-order harmonics, which are
not far away from the predominant mode and usually very strong.
In this section, different methods, including an embedded SRR and
metasurface layer, are combined to suppress the harmonic radiation
over a wide frequency range.
A. Embedded SRR
To suppress the radiation of the second-order harmonic, a SRR
is embedded into the PIFS, as shown in Fig. 7(a). The resonant
frequency of the SRR is tuned to the second-order harmonic of the
proposed ﬁltering antenna, at around 5.6 GHz. Fig. 8 compares the
simulated current distribution at 5.6 GHz between the Type-C and
Type-D antennas. As observed from Fig. 8(a), when the PIFS and
the parasitic strip resonators are working at the second-order mode,
intensive power can be coupled from PIFS to the strip resonators.
When the SRR is embedded into the PIFS, which is resonant at
around 5.6 GHz, an intensive current is distributed around the SRR.
Hence, the power coupled to the two parasitic strip resonators can be
signiﬁcantly reduced. Since the majority power is reﬂected back on
the PIFS, the second-order harmonic can be efﬁciently suppressed.
Fig. 9 compares the simulated peak realized gain and radiation
efﬁciency among the reference antennas Type-C, Type-D, Type-E,
and the proposed antenna. It is noted that the peak realized gain
instead of the realized gain in the broadside direction is adopted
to measure the harmonic suppression performance as the cross-band
interference may originally come from any direction, but not only
from the broadside direction. As observed from Fig. 9(a), the peak
realized gain of the second-order harmonic is reduced from 6 dBi to
below 0 dBi from the Type-C antenna to the Type-D antenna, and
the radiation efﬁciency is reduced from 40% to 14%.
B. Metasurface for Harmonic Suppression
Although most of the input power of the second-order harmonic is
reﬂected back at the PIFS, there are still some power couples from
the PIFS to the patch and radiate out. To further suppress unwanted
radiation, a new method of loading a layer of metasurface below the
radiator is proposed, as shown in Fig. 7(b). The metasurface is placed
on the upper layer of the bottom substrate without introducing addi-
tional substrate/layer. The conﬁguration of the unit cell is presented
in Fig. 10(a), which is simply a patch shorted to the ground plane
through a pin. The opened sides of the patch are equivalent to a
capacitor, whereas the shorted pin can be molded as an inductor; the
lossy substrate is represented by a resistor. Thus, the unit cell can
be viewed as a series resonant circuit, and the resonant frequency
can be controlled by tuning the gap between the unit cells. When it
resonates, an intensive E-ﬁeld distribution will be generated, leading
to the loss of power. As a result, the power in the designed frequency
can be suppressed [35].
A periodic boundary is used to investigate the resonance of the unit
cell, as shown in Fig. 10(b). As observed, the resonance is moved to
the lower band when L4 is increased. The resonance here indicates
that a small part of the incident wave is absorbed and lost in the unit
cell when it resonates, but it is insufﬁcient to deal with high-power
cases when it works alone, as the Type-E curve shown in Fig. 9.
However, this additional structure can be used to further suppress the
radiation in the given frequency range. As depicted in Fig. 9, the peak
realized gain at the second-order harmonic can be reduced by 14 dB
when rejection bands of the SRR and the metasurface are aligned with
each other. Analyzing the radiation efﬁciency in Fig. 9(b), the power
radiated out is further suppressed to below 4% when the metasurface
is applied, demonstrating that a good harmonic suppression can be
achieved.
For better presenting the harmonic suppression performance, the
simulated E-ﬁeld distributions of the antenna are displayed and com-
pared in Fig. 11. As shown in Fig. 11(a), although a major power of
the second-order harmonic has been reﬂected back at the input, there
are still some power coupled to the radiating patch, which is working
at its high-order mode. When the metasurface is placed below the
radiating patch, the power that is coupled to the radiating patch is
much weaker than that the one without a metasurface, as shown in
Fig. 11(b). Having another check of the E-ﬁeld distribution on the
upper layer of the bottom substrate, an intensive E-ﬁeld is distributed
along the gaps between the unit cell without producing an effective
radiation, which veriﬁes our supposition. Therefore, by combining
the embedded SRR in the PIFS and loading a layer of metasurface,
the radiation of the harmonics can be signiﬁcantly suppressed.
IV. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
The proposed ﬁltering antenna was fabricated, and the upper layers
of the bottom and top substrates of the prototype are respectively
shown in Fig. 12. As shown in Fig. 12(a), from inner to outer,
they are PIFS with embedded SRR, two parasitic strip resonators,
and a layer of metasurface surrounding. The copper areas of the
two layers are similar, and thus, a compact size can be maintained.
Fig. 13(a) presents the measured and simulated S-parameters from
1.5 to 9 GHz. As observed, the measured results agree well with
the simulations in terms of impedance match and gain response.
The measured impedance −10 dB bandwidth of the antenna is from
2.4 to 2.9 GHz. Outside of the band, the reﬂection coefﬁcients are
close to 0 dB. Fig. 13(b) displays the simulated and measured peak
realized gains and the radiation efﬁciency of the proposed ﬁltering
antenna. Similarly, a good consistence can be observed between the
simulated and measured results. As can be seen, the measured peak
realized gains are about 8 dBi in the band, which is quickly reduced
to below −15 dBi from 3 to 5.8 GHz, giving a harmonic suppression
of over 23 dB. The realized gain is somehow increased in the band of
6.0–9.0 GHz, but still remains over 18 dB gain suppression. This is
mainly due to the mismatch between the higher order resonance of the
patch and the PIFS. The minor discrepancy between the simulated
and measured results at around 6 GHz is mainly attributed to the
fabrication tolerances. Besides, the antenna has a high efﬁciency of
around 90% in the band, but it is basically remained below 8% out
of the band from 3.0 to 9.0 GHz, showing an excellent harmonic
suppression performance.
Fig. 14 shows the simulated and measured normalized radia-
tion patterns of the proposed antenna at 2.6 GHz. The antenna
exhibits uni-directional radiation pattern in the broadside direction.
The cross-polarization level is more than 30 dB lower than in the
co-polarization. In addition, the front-to-back ratio is over 20 dB,
showing the proposed antenna has a good radiation performance.
The small discrepancy between the simulated and measured radiation
patterns is mainly due to the tolerances during the measurement.
The proposed antenna is compared with other ﬁltering antennas
with harmonic suppression performance reported in [26], [27], [28],
[29], [30], [31], [32], [33], and [34] in terms of antenna proﬁle,
method of suppression, gain in-band, frequency selectivity, and gain
suppression. The antennas in [32] and [33] have a limited bandwidth
of suppression of less than 2 f0, without tackling the second-order
harmonics. The works in [26] and [27] have a wideband harmonic
suppression, but a low in-band gain of less than 3 dBi can be
achieved. The works in [28], [31], and [33] have a limited frequency
selectivity with the roll-off ratio less than 60 dB/GHz. The work

V. CONCLUSION
In this communication, a compact ﬁltering antenna with improved
frequency selectivity and wideband harmonic suppression has been
proposed for wireless applications. By conﬁguring a cross-coupling,
a radiation null can be realized at the band-edge for enhancing the
frequency selectivity. To suppress the radiation from harmonics over
a wide frequency range, a slit ring resonator is ﬁrst embedded into the
feed source. Then, a metasurface is employed to further reduce the
harmonic radiation for the ﬁrst time. The principles of generating
and controlling the radiation null, as well as the procedure of
suppressing harmonics, have been explained in detail. Compared with
other reported works, the proposed ﬁltering antenna has shown an
improved frequency selectivity and wideband harmonic suppression
performance. The techniques developed in this work can be widely
used in other types of antennas.
